opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
Today I sat with a question that has been bothering me: why would Jesus curse a fig tree? He approaches it hungry. It has leaves. It looks alive. It looks fruitful. Yet there is nothing there. What unsettles me most is that Scripture itself says it was not the season for figs. So why curse something for not producing what the season itself did not require?
Then Jesus enters Jerusalem. He overturns tables, blocks traffic through the temple, calls it a den of thieves, and immediately after this, teaches about faith, prayer, and forgiveness. Believe when you pray. Forgive others so your Father may forgive you. At first, I am bothered by this. Why curse the tree? Why overturn tables? Why show anger while teaching faith? The train of thought feels disconnected until perhaps it isn’t.
Maybe the fig tree was never about agriculture. The leaves suggested promise. From a distance, it appeared fruitful. Up close, there was nothing. Appearance without fruit. Then comes the temple, and perhaps it too had leaves: ritual, sacrifice, crowds, commerce, religious activity. Yet Christ finds little fruit there either. Suddenly, the fig tree and the temple seem less like separate moments and more like the same lesson repeated twice. Christ confronting what appears alive but no longer gives life.
And if I am honest, this is where fear enters. Because I read this and immediately place myself where the tree stands.
I have not borne the fruit I hoped I would. I stay home more than I should. I avoid things sometimes because being around people while still feeling alone is exhausting. I pray for fruit while simultaneously wondering whether, if given it, I would even know what to do with it. I worry because I do not feel particularly fruitful. I worry about what becomes of people who feel more like roots than branches.
Then another thought comes. A fruitless tree does not worry about fruit. I do. I wrestle. I ask. I doubt. I return. I continue searching. And maybe that matters.
Jesus begins this entire scene hungry. Perhaps the deeper question is not whether I have produced enough fruit, but whether I am still responding to the hunger for God. Because when Jesus speaks about prayer, He immediately speaks about forgiveness. When He speaks about faith, He speaks about transformation. Prayer without forgiveness is leaves. Religion without communion is leaves. Appearance without transformation is leaves.
Maybe fruit is quieter than I imagined. Maybe fruit is continuing to pray while uncertain, showing up while lonely, forgiving when hurt, remaining open when exhausted, or continuing to seek God when it would be easier not to.
I still do not fully understand the fig tree. Perhaps that is because I keep standing where the tree stands — afraid, wondering if there is enough fruit, wondering what becomes of me.
And maybe Christ’s hunger is not only judgment.
Maybe it is an invitation.
